newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Royalists appeal for aid for Cambodian refugees.
newsitem.headline: Royalists appeal for aid for Cambodian refugees.

text.p: Thousands of Cambodian refugees fleeing fighting in the war-torn country's north have sought refuge in this town held by forces of ousted FUNCINPEC leader and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

A local FUNCINPEC official told Reuters many of the 12,544 refugees, mostly women and children, were sick and that food was short. He appealed for foreign aid for the displaced, who are poised to cross the border into Thailand, if allowed.
"The people escaped from fighting in Samrong, Chongkal and Srey Snom. Many of them have brought nothing along with them," said Rom Tekkhak Muny, chief administrator of the town.
"They are now facing food and medicine shortages. We are appealing to the international community to give us assistance," he said. "We urgently need food, medicine and plastic sheets."
The refugees have fled fighting between FUNCINPEC soldiers and those loyal to strongman and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who overthrew Ranariddh in a bloody coup earlier this month.
Hun Sen's men are fighting to take over control of towns still held by FUNCINPEC forces throughout the country.

Those in O'Smach represent a fraction of the thousands of Cambodian refugees stuck at the Thai-Cambodian border, an American non-governmental agency called the U.S. Committee for Refugees said in a statement received in Bangkok.
Thai authorities have so far refused to allow the refugees to cross the border.
"Thailand is denying them entry and asylum and prohibiting the UN High Commissioner for Refugees from going to the border to assess the situation," said the American group.
The O'Smach refugees live in makeshift shelters, under plastic sheets and bushes.

Thida Hong, a mother of three children who fled from Samrong to live under a two-square-metre plastic sheet, told Reuters that her three year old son had the flu for two days, but she had no money to buy medicine for him.

Sithy Men, a Cambodian doctor who fled from Phnom Penh one week after Hun Sen's forces crushed FUNCINPEC loyalists in the capital, said more than 100 people came to use outpatient services in his makeshift clinic in the area.
"There are 38 people who are suffering from malaria and diarrhoea warded in my clinic," he said. "Now we are running out of the medicine. We need help from the foreign countries.

Sithy Men, the only doctor in the 10-bed, makeshift hospital roofed with pieces of cloth and grass, said that in just three days he had used up all 7,000 medicine tablets received from Medicines Sans Frontiers, a French non-government organisation.
He said he was building another makeshift hospital, but was in dire need of foreign assistance.
"These people are too scared to return to their villages for the time being. So we have to keep them here until the situation is back to normal," said the town administrator Rom.
"But the problem is we do not have food and other necessary supplies to help them. We hope that the international community will come in the help us," he added.
